bio.en: Ben Lauzier was VP of Product and Growth at Thumbtack (3x growth in three years) and an early Lyft employee (#30) who led driver-side product and growth, and now advises marketplace teams and founded healthcare startup Nurra.
bio.zh: Ben Lauzier 曾任 Thumbtack 产品与增长副总裁（三年内增长 3 倍），也是 Lyft 早期员工（第 30 号），负责司机端产品与增长，现为正念市场团队顾问，并创办了医疗创业公司 Nurra。

summary.en: Ben goes deep on building and scaling marketplaces: what to focus on pre-product-market fit, which side to prioritize, how to track liquidity, and what causes most marketplaces to fail. He advocates providing guardrails and empowering supply rather than micromanaging from an ivory tower, plus clever supply-side growth tactics. The conversation also contrasts the European and U.S. product markets and what European companies should change.
summary.zh: Ben 深入探讨了构建和扩展双边市场：产品市场匹配前要关注什么、优先哪一侧、如何追踪流动性，以及大多数市场失败的原因。他主张提供护栏、赋能供给侧，而非坐在象牙塔里微观管理，并分享巧妙的供给侧增长策略。对话还对比了欧洲与美国产品市场，以及欧洲公司应做出哪些改变。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I think when you're running a marketplace, you tend to sit in your ivory tower a little bit, looking at stats and thinking like, "If only we could get people to do X, it'd be better for everyone." I certainly did that in my career. I think that's missing the point that we're humans, and I think sometimes we act in ways that are non-deterministic or counterintuitive. But my take is I'm a huge believer in market forces and empowerment, so provide guardrails for what a good experience is in your marketplace, set a clear bar for quality, and provide the right coaching and tools for supply to be successful, and then take a step back and see where the gaps are and invest more in hands-on tactics just to close those gaps more specifically.
turns.zh: 我认为，当你运营一个市场平台时，人们往往会陷入自以为是的境地，盯着数据分析，幻想"只要能让用户做到某件事，一切就会变得更好"。我在职业生涯中也曾犯过这样的错误。但我认为，我们忽略了一个关键点——人终究是感性的，有时会做出非理性或反直觉的决策。不过我的观点是，我深信市场力量和赋权的重要性。所以，要为你的市场平台构建清晰的用户体验标准，设定明确的质量门槛，为供应商提供成功所需的指导和工具，然后退后一步，观察差距并投入更多精力开展实操策略来精准弥补这些漏洞。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today my guest is Ben Lauzier. Prior to Thumbtack, Ben was at Lyft for over six years, where he was employee number 30 and led product and growth for the driver's side of the business, and at one point reached 1% of U.S. workers driving for Lyft every month. He currently spends his time advising marketplace teams and founders, teaching a reforged course on marketplace growth, and most recently started a healthcare company called Nurra that connects you to a care advocate to help you navigate the healthcare system in the U.S. In our conversation, we go many layers deep on the many key elements of building and scaling a marketplace business, including what to focus on pre-product market fit, how to know which side of the marketplace to prioritize, what product market fit looks like, how to track liquidity, what causes most marketplaces to fail and how to avoid that. (00:01:43): And a bunch of examples of really clever growth strategies, especially on the supply side, and some really interesting stories about how Lyft was able to compete with Uber early on with one-tenth of the resources. As a bonus, Ben also shares insights into how the European product market is different from the U.S. product market, and what he encourages European companies to change in order to operate more effectively and be more innovative. This episode is for anyone building or thinking about building a marketplace business. If you enjoy this podcast, don't forget to subscribe and follow it in your favorite podcasting app or YouTube, it's the best way to avoid missing future episodes and it helps the podcast tremendously. turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I mean, like you mentioned, I love marketplaces. turns.zh: 就像你提到的，我非常喜欢市场型业务。我从事市场型业务的搭建和扩展工作已经快15年了，我觉得它们为我们作为产品经理所面临的挑战增添了一个极具吸引力的维度。当你深入研究市场型业务时，你会发现一些隐藏的深层逻辑。从理论上讲，市场型业务的定义很简单：由两个或多个相互独立的参与方组成，他们为彼此创造价值，然后由一个中介机构来促成这种价值交换。这样解释很清晰。但在实际操作中，边界往往更模糊。市场型业务存在诸多有趣的维度，比如中介机构的介入程度如何，这决定了市场型业务的管理程度。例如，Craigslist就属于完全放任、缺乏管理的类型；而Lyft则开始走向半监管模式，平台会深度参与价值交换过程。以上就是我的理解，不过市场型业务还有很多引人入胜的变体。

turns.zh: 完全正确。是的，是的。我认为，再次强调，有些公司声称自己是管理型市场平台，但这取决于你的视角——比如从投资者的角度看，你可能会选择不同的角度，但这就进入灰色地带了。但没错，市场平台的核心概念是公司不拥有供应方资源。从某种意义上说，这就是市场平台与单纯销售产品的区别所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so let's come back to that, because that's a really important topic and it's something that every marketplace trends towards or thinks about is just like we're going to control the supply, we're going to manage it, we're going to maybe own it in the future, but let's get back to that. So, you work with a ton of marketplaces, you've built a bunch of marketplaces. What do you find is the biggest struggle to building a successful marketplace business? The most common problem people run into.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们再回过头来讨论这个话题，因为这确实是个非常重要的话题。每个市场平台都倾向于或思考着如何控制供应、管理供应，甚至未来可能自主拥有供应，但我们先回归正题。你与众多市场平台合作过，也亲自打造过不少平台。在打造成功的市场平台业务时，你认为最大的挑战是什么？人们最常遇到的难题是什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I think there's two types of challenges, I guess there's when you're talking about creating a marketplace, and then there's when you're talking about scaling a marketplace. For creating a marketplace, I see many founders that are pre-product market fit, super eager to nerd out on marketplace dynamics. They're super excited to launch a marketplace, we all are, and they want to talk about supply and demand, they want to look at all kinds of ratios. They show me economic papers and ask, "How could we apply this principle to my company?" And here, my advice is generally always, "If you don't have product market fit, and if you don't have a good enough growth strategy for at least one side of your marketplace, just forget about all this marketplace stuff." (00:08:46): Focus on this core exchange of value, go deep with one side of the marketplace and see if you can rely on some crutch, some hack for the other side for time being. And you see companies like Airbnb and Thumbtack doing this with Craigslist pretty early on to jumpstart their growth as just countless examples, but don't get distracted by this shiny and cool intellectually challenging idea of working on the marketplace, and nail the basics of your product market fit at first.
turns.zh: 我认为挑战主要分为两类：一是创建市场平台，二是扩大市场平台规模。就创建市场平台而言，我发现许多创始人在产品市场匹配阶段就过度沉迷于市场动态。他们对推出市场平台充满热情，我们都一样，但他们总想探讨供需关系、分析各种比率指标。他们给我看经济学论文，问：“如何将这些原理应用到我们的公司？”对此，我的建议通常是：“如果产品市场匹配度不足，且至少一方的增长策略不完善，那就先别纠结于市场平台的复杂事宜。”（00:08:46）先专注于核心价值交换，深耕市场平台的一方业务，同时暂且为另一方业务寻找临时解决方案。Airbnb和Thumbtack早期就通过这种策略迅速启动增长，这只是无数成功案例中的两个例子。切勿被市场平台这种看似高大上、充满智力挑战的想法分心，先把产品市场匹配的基本功练好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, just to spend a little more time there to make this even more real. So, you're saying that pre-product market fit, before you find that anyone really wants what you're building, focus on figuring out a way to grow one side of the marketplace. So, maybe just two quick follow up questions. How do you know which side to focus on initially? And can you give an example, I think Thumbtack may be a good example of this, of how they did that?
turns.zh: 再具体说一下。你的意思是，在产品市场匹配度不足、尚未确定用户对产品需求之前，重点在于找到增长某一方的方法。那么我有两个快速跟进的问题：如何判断最初该专注于哪一方？能否举个例子？Thumbtack或许就是个很好的案例。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Which side to focus on is there's different approaches to this, but generally people will pick the hardest side. And so, I'll take the example of Thumbtack, because we're going to talk about it. So, Thumbtack is a home services marketplace to help you find plumbers, electricians, and the harder side there was demand. There's supply, and you can look for, you can open the yellow pages, you can find plumbers somewhere, but the hardest question was can we go out there and can we find people who want to do something in their house, who have projects that need to be done? What is the core growth strategy for us to acquire those people, to find them? And what kind of retention can we create? Can we create a delightful experience for them to come back to our platform and want us to take care of their home for them? (00:10:32): Pick the hardest side is my advice. And then, how some companies do this, again, I think there's a lot of different ways to do this, but a common advice is find a way to jumpstart one side. Find a way to hack one side, play one player mode is what it's also called sometimes, but try to find a way to tap into existing channels that have one side of your marketplace already latent. And so again, you have countless businesses that if you've been built off of Craigslist, I think Thumbtack was partially one of them, and the idea was like, "Hey, we can find all those great pros on Thumbtack. When we have someone who wants a job, 'Oh, you want your kitchen remodeled?' We can, behind the scenes, go and post a job on Craigslist and then we'll bring on all the contractors who are browsing Craigslist looking for jobs, we'll bring them to our platform." (00:11:26): That's an example of how that you worry about the core value proposition of can we get people to come back to the platform? Can we create this delightful exchange of value? Are people trusting us? Do we have the right checks in place to make sure that you are hiring the right person? What will make you come back? And once that's done, then you can focus around how do I build a flywheel on the supply side, and how do I manage and how do I make sure I have enough plumbers per market, or something like that.
turns.zh:
选择哪个方面作为重点存在不同的方法，但通常人们会选择最困难的那个面。以Thumbtack为例，因为我们要重点讨论它。Thumbtack是一个家居服务平台，帮助用户寻找水管工、电工等专业人员。在供需关系中，供给方面相对容易——你可以翻阅黄页、在某处寻找水管工，但最难的问题在于：我们能否主动出击，找到那些有房屋翻修需求、需要完成项目的人？我们的核心增长策略是什么？如何获取这些用户？如何提升用户留存率？如何为他们创造愉快的体验，让他们愿意再次使用我们的平台？（00:10:32）：我的建议是选择最困难的方面。有些公司会采取不同的策略，比如先突破其中一方，找到突破口。有时这被称为"玩家模式"，即利用现有渠道的潜力来快速启动某一侧市场。例如，许多基于Craigslist建立的公司（Thumbtack就是其中之一）会这样做："我们在Thumbtack上汇聚了优秀的专业人员。当有人需要厨房翻修时，我们可以在幕后将需求发布到Craigslist上，然后吸引正在Craigslist上寻找工作的承包商加入我们的平台。"
（00:11:26）：这启示我们要关注核心价值主张：能否让用户持续回访平台？能否创造愉快的价值交换？用户是否信任我们？我们是否有合适的机制确保聘请到合适的人才？怎样才能让用户再次光顾？一旦这些问题得到解决，再去考虑如何在供给侧建立增长飞轮，如何管理并确保每个市场都有足够的专业人员等问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say find the hard side, how do you find that? Any advice you can give founders and teams?
turns.zh: 你提到要找到最困难的方面，那具体怎么找呢？对创始人和团队有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: In general, I would say intuitively the teams know, especially the teams are in the weeds, they know. They know, "Well, yeah, we can get X. But what we really struggle with is getting students to look at this." That's your sign. And I think sometimes it takes someone else to make you think about it, to reflect like, "Actually, yes, you're right. This side is obvious. We know how to get it, we just don't have the right supply for it and we don't know where to find the supply." Boom, that's the side that you should be focused on. Then you find a way to add source to demand, subsidize it, find some other way, and focus on this side that you have no idea how to grow. You should have a reliable growth strategy for the side.
turns.zh: 通常来说，我认为团队直觉上就能意识到这一点，尤其是在陷入困境的团队，他们很清楚。"嗯，我们能获取X，但真正难的是让学生群体关注到这里。"这就是信号。我觉得有时需要其他人来提醒你反思，比如"其实没错，这方面很明显，我们知道怎么做，但就是没有合适的供给渠道"。然后就把注意力集中在最难增长的方面。接着想办法增加供需对接、提供补贴或寻找其他解决方案，专注于这个你毫无头绪的增长侧面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In my experience, it's almost always the supply side is what you need to work on, because once you have awesome supply, people are going to be really excited to tap it. Like Uber drivers, Airbnb homes, professionals on Thumbtack. Is that your experience too?
turns.zh: 以我的经验来看，通常需要优先优化供给侧，因为一旦有优质的供给，用户就会迫不及待地想要使用。比如Uber司机、Airbnb房源、Thumbtack上的专业人员。你们也有同样的经验吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yes. I would say supply is the hardest side maybe like 80% to 90% of the time. Yeah, I totally agree. I was trying to think of counter examples, but I can't think of one. I just know that there are.
turns.zh: 是的。我得说，在大多数情况下，供应方都是最难解决的部分，比例可能高达80%到90%。是的，我完全同意。我试图想出反例，但实在想不出来。只是我知道确实存在这样的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's one I know, which is Rover, based on research I did, because it turned out it was really easy to find people who want to walk dogs and watch dogs for 50 bucks an hour or whatever. It was a very easy value prop, and so they had a waitlist, they had just so many people. Also, TaskRabbit is the one I know about where they had so many people wanting to be taskers, whatever they call them-
turns.zh: 有个例子，我知道Rover就是这样。根据我做的研究，他们发现想找人遛狗、看狗的人特别多，收费每小时50美元左右。这是一个非常简单的价值主张，结果他们甚至有等候名单，需求量太大了。还有TaskRabbit这个平台，我也了解到，他们也有很多人想成为任务执行者——不管他们怎么称呼这些人——

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I was going to mention TaskRabbit as well. I heard of that as well, yeah.
turns.zh: 我本来也想提到TaskRabbit的。我也听说过这个平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then you talked about there's a core part of figuring out how to grow that part, how to grow the hard part, generally the supply side. You shared a couple examples. Are there any more clever things you recall that you might be able to share of just ways people grew supply early on that could inspire people that are trying to figure this out right now?
turns.zh: 好的。然后你提到，要想办法增长供应方，特别是供应方这块难题。刚才你分享了几个例子。还有其他更巧妙的做法吗？比如早期如何吸引供应方，哪些方法能给现在正为此头疼的人带来启发？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a couple of common tactics I would say pretty early on that I think companies rely on. So, we've talked about jump-starting one side of the marketplace with, it may be with Thumbtack and Lyft, also leverage job boards. You have also a lot of companies building value added services pretty early on as a core way of retaining supply pretty early on. Like let's build a really compelling basket of value for this supply, and this is going to be the thing that appeals everyone. So, OpenTable did this really well with all the restaurant services, other things that I've seen people use really well early on or converting your supply into demand or demand into supply pretty early on, so Lyft, we tried that. It actually didn't work at Lyft, but I know other marketplaces have been pretty successful with that.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得早期有几个常见策略，公司都会用到。比如快速启动某一方市场，比如Thumbtack和Lyft，还有利用招聘网站。还有很多公司早期就开发增值服务，作为留住供应方的核心手段。比如为供应方打造极具吸引力的价值组合，这样能吸引所有人。OpenTable在餐饮服务方面就做得很好，还有其他我见过的早期成功案例，比如将供应转化为需求，或将需求转化为供应。Lyft就尝试过这种方法，但没成功，不过其他平台在这方面做得很成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make sure people understand that one, it's a really interesting one is, in the Lyft example would be convincing drivers to become riders, convincing riders to become drivers, and mostly the latter, convincing riders to become drivers.
turns.zh: 确保大家理解一点，Lyft的例子很有意思。早期要说服司机成为乘客，乘客成为司机，但主要还是后者，要说服乘客成为司机。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. In our case at Lyft early on, we had a waitlist on the demand side because we just couldn't onboard enough supply. And so, we had this idea of having a pop-up. Instead of saying no drivers available, it would be like, "Hey, sorry, all the drivers are taken. People are making 50 bucks an hour right now, do you want to hop on your car and drive?" And we had some conversions, but it felt a little distracting to the overall experience and it wasn't a huge driver of supply. But I know that for Uber it actually was. I think they had a relatively meaningful amount of supply coming from [inaudible 00:15:27]
turns.zh: 对，确实。早期在Lyft，我们因为供应方不足，在需求方也排起了长队。于是我们想到了一个临时措施。不是说司机没空，而是改成“抱歉，司机名额已满。现在司机时薪50美元，你想开车吗？”这样确实有转化，但对整体体验有点干扰，也没能有效增加供应量。不过我知道Uber在这方面做得不错。我记得他们有相当数量的供应来自[此处不清]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, how does that make you feel that Uber figured out a better way to approach this and made it work? That doesn't feel-
turns.zh: 哇，Uber找到了更好的解决办法，这让你感觉如何？这感觉不太容易——

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: And it's a different audience. You would think that the Lyft passenger and driver is more likely to flip back and forth between the two. I don't know, I don't know. [inaudible 00:15:47]
turns.zh: 而且目标人群不同。你可能会觉得Lyft的乘客和司机更容易互换角色。我也不确定，[此处不清00:15:47]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, a PM at Uber outdid you guys. Oh, no.
turns.zh: 是的，Uber的某位产品经理比你们做得更好。哦，不。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yes, on a couple of other things.
turns.zh: 是的，还有其他几件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有意思。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: And we outdid them on a few other things [inaudible 00:15:55]
turns.zh: 而且我们在其他几方面也超越了他们 [00:15:55听不清]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, okay. That's right. So, essentially what we've been spending some time on here is just when you're starting a marketplace, figure out which side you need to drive, because that's what will unlock this opportunity. There's a hard thing that nobody's ever done before, and most of the time it's build a bunch of supply that nobody has done before, and there's all these tactics to do that. And all of this is, as you coming back to the main question I asked, we've gone on this awesome tangent, is pre-product market fit before you even know this is a thing. Spend time most of the time building supply to see if demand, customers actually want this thing. Right?
turns.zh: 好的，好的。没错。所以，我们在这里花时间讨论的主要问题是，当你启动一个市场平台时，要明确你需要推动哪一方的发展，因为这才是解锁机遇的关键。有一个难题是之前没人做过的，大多数时候需要建立大量供应，而这需要各种策略。回到我最初的问题，所有这些讨论都围绕着一个核心点——在你甚至还没意识到这是一个机会之前，就要先验证产品与市场的适配度。大部分时间都花在建立供应上，看看需求是否存在，客户是否真的需要这个产品。对吧？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Exactly. And then I think there's a different set of challenges. The other pitfall that I see is, so pre-product market fit, people tend to be distracted by those marketplace dynamics like we talked about instead of doing what we just talked about. For companies that have some sort of scale and product market fit, to me the place where I see people getting tripped up most often is the concept of marketplace liquidity or how to match the health of a marketplace. To me, liquidity is how marketplaces win. It's this measure of your ability to match buyers and sellers efficiently, it's how quickly and efficiently people can find what they're looking for on your platform. So, you can picture a Venn diagram. One circle is this is what supply wants to sell, and another circle is this is what demand wants to buy, and your liquidity is the overlap between those two circles. (00:17:26): So for, let's take the example of Lyft or Uber, because we talked about them. It might be for all the people who open the app with the intention to book a ride, how many of those actually turn into a ride? And this metric liquidity, it's a direct multiplier on the efficiency of your marketplace. It's literally at the center of your vision, it's why you exist as a marketplace is to connect the two. And it's also the ultimate engagement loop. The more supply you have, the more choice people have, the better the services, the more likely it is that it turns into a transaction and the more likely it is that they come back. And so, it's really this incredible circle. And what I see is people missing how critical this component is in the marketplace, struggle to define it for the business, and most importantly struggle to build an actionable playbook against it. Like, "Okay, how do I manage this? Okay, it's important, but what do I do about it?" Basically.
turns.zh: 没错。我认为还有另一组挑战。我看到的另一个陷阱是，关于产品与市场适配度的前期验证，人们往往会被我们讨论过的市场平台动态所分心，忽略了我们刚刚讨论的内容。对于已经有一定规模和产品市场适配度的公司来说，我认为他们最常遇到的难题是市场平台的流动性概念，或者如何衡量一个市场平台的健康度。对我来说，流动性是市场平台获胜的关键。这是衡量你高效匹配买家和卖家的能力的指标，也是人们在你的平台上快速高效找到所需物品的能力。所以，你可以想象一个维恩图。一个圆圈是供应方想卖的东西，另一个圆圈是需求方想买的东西，而流动性就是这两个圆圈的重叠部分。（00:17:26）：以Lyft或Uber为例，因为我们讨论过它们。可能是所有打开应用打算预订乘车服务的人中，实际成功预订的比例有多少？这个流动性指标直接决定了市场平台的效率。它是你的愿景核心，也是你作为市场平台存在的意义——连接买家和卖家。它还是最终的用户参与循环。供应越多，选择越多，服务越好，成交概率越高，回访率也越高。这真是一个良性循环。我发现人们没有意识到这个关键因素对市场平台的重要性，难以为业务定义它，最重要的是难以制定针对它的可行策略。比如，“好的，我该如何管理这个问题？好吧，它很重要，但我该怎么做？”基本上就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a metric you recommend people specifically look at to understand liquidity?
turns.zh: 有没有你特别推荐人们关注的衡量流动性的指标？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I think the metric that I like the most is a predictor of liquidity. So your liquidity might be, it's typically a measure of demand utilization. It might be looking for something on there, maybe how many of those searches with intent actually turn into a transaction. So, it's your field rate of your intentful demand typically, and that's really indicative of the net output of your marketplace. And so, that gives you a sense of the health of your marketplace, but it can be influenced by a whole bunch of different factors. So, if you think about for Thumbtack, it can be influenced by if there's a snowstorm out there, if the competition is bidding, there's a whole bunch of exogenous factors that come into play. And the metric that I think is slightly more actionable is a little harder to define, but so much more helpful in my opinion. (00:19:19): It's what I call a market health metric, and this is basically think of your proxy that is the best predictor of your liquidity. So, I'll use the example of Lyft. You have your liquidity is your demand utilization, it's how many app opens turn into a ride, and what predicts this? What will predict you and deciding to book a ride? For Lyft and for Uber, it was ETAs. So, we knew that if the closest driver was at least two minutes away from you or closer, then we had hit a ceiling, you were more than X person likely to convert and book a ride. If it's more than two minutes, if it's five, then maybe you check at Uber, maybe you walk, maybe you take the bus. If it's two minutes, it doesn't make a big enough difference, you're just going to book the ride anyway. (00:20:06): So find this threshold, find this predictor that tends to plateau that correlates strongly with retention but with also the transaction happening, and that's the metric that you can predict. That's a metric that's so much more actionable for teams to work against. If you're a supply team now you can think of, "Okay, I'm adding 100 supplies into the platform. I want to know if it's actually reducing ETAs in this case," or I can look at correlations like this and limiting some of the effect of those exhaustive factors that I mentioned.
turns.zh: 我认为我最喜欢的指标是流动性预测器。因此，你的流动性通常是需求利用率的衡量标准。它可能需要观察用户的搜索行为，比如有多少带有实际交易意图的搜索最终转化为实际交易。所以，这基本上是你的领域内需求意图的转化率，而这也正是你市场净产出的重要指标。通过它，你可以了解市场健康状况，但它会受到诸多因素的影响。比如，Thumbtack平台的流动性就可能受雪天天气、竞争对手出价等外部因素影响。而在我看来，更具可操作性的指标虽然更难定义，但却更有实际价值。（00:19:19）我称之为市场健康度指标，它本质上是预测流动性的最佳指标。以Lyft为例，你的流动性就是需求利用率，即打开应用后转化为乘车订单的比例。那么，什么因素能预测用户是否会决定预订乘车服务呢？对于Lyft和Uber来说，关键指标是到达时间估算（ETA）。我们发现，如果距离用户最近的司机距离超过两分钟或更远，那么转化率就会达到上限，用户转化为订单的概率会显著降低。如果超过两分钟，比如五分钟，用户可能会去Uber平台看看，或者选择步行或乘坐公交车。但如果两分钟以内，用户转化概率就会大大增加，最终还是会选择预订乘车服务。（00:20:06）因此，找到这个阈值，找到这个与留存率高度相关、同时与交易转化率紧密相关的预测指标，这才是可预测的关键指标。这对团队来说更有实际操作价值。例如，如果你现在是供应团队，你可以思考：“我要在平台上增加100个供应商，我想知道这是否真的能缩短到达时间。”或者你可以分析类似的相关性，并减轻我提到的那些复杂因素的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So, essentially watch fill rate is the term used that a lot of people love, which is just people with intent converting. So, the Airbnb example is exactly the way we did Airbnb is we looked at people that are searching with dates as intentful users, and then how many of them convert to a booking. So, that's basically what you're trying to get to, and your point here is that's kind of the output metric. That's what you want to move, but in order to move it, there's something that is the biggest lever to moving fill rate. And in your experience, and I've seen this exact same thing, it's usually amount of supply. Do you have enough good supply? And so, in the case of Lyft is do you have enough cars? Do you have enough homes, do you have enough plumbers on Thumbtack? And that's usually where you can actually impact fill rate. Sweet.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以，本质上，观察填充率是很多人喜欢使用的术语，指的是有意向的用户转化为实际行动。比如Airbnb的例子，我们正是通过将搜索带有日期的人视为有意向的用户，然后观察其中有多少人最终转化为预订。这基本上就是你要达到的目标，而你的观点是，这才是输出指标。这才是你想要提升的关键，但要提升它，最重要的杠杆就是供应量。你的供应充足吗？在Lyft案例中，就是车源充足吗？在Thumbtack上，就是水管工的供应充足吗？而这通常是影响填充率的关键。太好了。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that becomes the goal of the team, that becomes the focus of the company, basically drive that up in all the little markets you're in and all the categories you're in.
turns.zh: 这就成了团队的目标，成为公司的焦点，基本上就是要在你所涉及的所有小市场和类别中提升这一指标。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Exactly. Yeah, completely.
turns.zh: 没错。是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You mentioned this idea of product market fit and the things change, pre-product market fit, post-product market fit. Classic question, I'm curious if you have any insights here, just what tells you that you've climbed that hill of product market fit, that you might have product market fit, or you definitely have product market fit in a marketplace?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到了产品市场契合度这个概念，以及产品市场契合度前后期的变化。这是个经典问题，想问问你有没有什么深刻见解，怎样判断自己已经达到了产品市场契合度的巅峰？又或者说，在某个市场中你肯定已经达到了产品市场契合度？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: It's hard because to me, the two are most independent. Maybe this is a hot take, but I feel like product market fit is independent of your marketplace dynamics. You might have a great product, and it provides amazing value to both sides, but you have yet to crack the flywheel on the supply side for how to bring those people. You don't have the right product channel fit, for example. And so, this will have a massive impact on the dynamics of your marketplace. And so, to me, my answer would tend to be pretty classical, it would be like measure your product market fit the way you would for a normal company. So yeah, it's a bit of an art more than the science, but I like the classic if we were to take this product away, what percentage of users would be significantly disappointed or have no other solution? (00:22:50): So, questions like this I think go to the heart of how valuable is your solution to users, and you can do this on the supply side and the demand side. I think here my advice is typically to consider that you have two product market fits essentially. You want to make sure that you have a compelling enough value proposition on both sides of the marketplace, and very often at the beginning you find product market fit on the demand side, but you realize it's not compelling enough for your suppliers because your margins are too high or something like that. So, realizing that you have both those things, but I think you can measure them in a way that's relatively traditional, and that's independent of marketplace dynamics.
turns.zh: 这确实挺难的，因为在我看来，两者是高度独立的。或许这算个非主流观点，但我觉得产品市场契合度和市场动态是相互独立的。你可能拥有一款很棒的产品，能为双方创造巨大价值，但你尚未在供应端破解如何吸引用户的难题，比如产品渠道契合度不够完善。这就会对市场动态产生巨大影响。所以对我来说，答案往往比较传统——用普通公司的方法衡量产品市场契合度。没错，这更多是门艺术而非科学，但我还是倾向于用经典方法：如果把产品撤出市场，会有多少用户会深感失望或无处可去？（00:22:50）这类问题能直击解决方案对用户的价值所在，你可以在供应端和需求端分别进行评估。我通常建议从本质上看待产品市场契合度：你需要确保市场两端都能获得足够有力的价值主张。初期你可能在需求端发现产品市场契合度，但随后发现供应端对此不买账，比如利润率过高等问题。关键在于意识到两者都需要评估，而且评估方法相对传统，与市场动态无关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. We actually just had Sean Ellis on the podcast talking about that exact survey, the Sean Ellis test of asking people how disappointed would you be if they left, if the product didn't exist. And I just love that you keep coming back to this point that I 100% agree with, that most of the challenges you have with a marketplace business, 90% are the same challenges you'll have with a non-marketplace business. And people over-focus on, "Oh, I need to think of this like a marketplace, and all the marketplace science behind all this stuff." And really it's all the same stuff every founder is dealing with product market fit, except you have two sides of it growth strategy, but you have two sides of it. So, I love that you keep going back to that. (00:24:10): Something that I definitely want to touch on is when people are thinking about starting a marketplace company, what are signals that a marketplace is a good model for the idea? Because I think a lot of people come into and be like, "I want to build a marketplace. Oh, I'm going to connect these two sides. It's going to be great," and there's no marketplace in this business, in this vertical. What are signs that marketplace dynamic and a business model is right for an idea versus no, it's not?
turns.zh: 太赞了。我们刚在播客上请了肖恩·埃利斯，他谈到的那项调查——让用户回答如果产品消失会多失望。这正是我一直强调的观点：市场平台业务90%的挑战和非平台业务如出一辙。太多人过于关注“我得把这当成平台来思考，研究平台科学”，而忽略了每个创始人都面临的核心挑战——产品市场契合度。不过平台业务有两端：增长策略需要同时考虑两端。这点你反复强调太棒了。（00:24:10）我想重点探讨一下，当人们考虑创办平台公司时，如何判断某个创意适合平台模式？因为很多人一上来就说：“我想做个平台，把两端连接起来，肯定很棒”，结果却发现所在行业根本没有平台可用。如何判断某个创意适合平台模式而非其他模式？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: No one ever say like, "Oh, I'm going to build Airbnb for X," it's not something that people say. I think the signs that come to mind are one, higher fragmentation. I think you want this long tail of buyers and sellers without a handful of big players controlling the market, because this is where you can provide value by doing this job of aggregation. I think you also want a relatively uniform set of needs. That means that it can be, like your supply can be commoditized to some extent. This is what's so tricky, by the way, about services, service marketplaces like Thumbtack, because unlike eBay, where sellers, they just want to sell very clear and distinct inventory, on Thumbtack you have electricians who only want certain types of jobs, but they only want it if they're available that day. And they might take a job and cancel it because something better comes up. (00:25:34): And so, this makes for a very fuzzy definition of supply, and you have very different set of needs. One electrician wants something, the other one has a very different perception of the same unit of demand, and that makes it very, very difficult. So, it's feasible, but I would say that is not a compelling attribute for building a marketplace. So, a relatively uniform set of needs. And the last one I'd mention is a high enough bearer in the matchmaking or the creation. I think how hard it is for people to find each other today, and how much effort do they have to put in to vet each other, I think is another great sign. The higher it is, the bigger the opportunity because it means you come in, implement the right processes to simplify this exchange of value.
turns.zh: 没人会说：“哦，我要为X打造Airbnb。”这种说法根本不常见。我认为关键的三个信号是：首先，市场高度碎片化。我希望买卖双方的数量足够分散，不被少数大平台把控，因为这样才能通过整合服务来创造价值。其次，要有相对统一的需求。这意味着供应可以一定程度上标准化。顺便说一句，服务类平台比如Thumbtack就很棘手，因为不像eBay上的卖家只需出售清晰明确的商品，Thumbtack上的电工可能只接收特定类型的订单，但前提是当天有空档。有些订单甚至可能因有更合适的机会而被取消。（00:25:34）这就导致供应定义模糊不清，需求也千差万别。一位电工可能需要某种服务，而另一位对同一需求却有截然不同的理解，这无疑增加了挑战。因此，虽然可行，但我认为这并非打造市场平台的核心要素。第三，匹配或撮合的门槛足够高。我注意到如今人们寻找彼此的难度极大，验证信任的成本也极高。这恰恰说明市场潜力巨大，越是高门槛，就越意味着巨大的机遇，因为这意味着你可以通过合理流程简化价值交换。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'd love to know if there's any examples you can think of, of bad marketplace ideas that people have tried, but I'll summarize the three points you just made, which I love. So, these are signs that this is a great opportunity for marketplace business, that there's a lot of fragmentation on both sides. There's not just a small number of companies or customers on one side or the other, because if there are, why do they need you? There's five airlines or whatever, you don't need a marketplace to match with an airline. Then two is there's uniform needs, the needs are basically consistent. I just want to stay in a home, I want a car to take me somewhere, I want a plumber. (00:27:04): And then there's a barrier, there's complexity to the matchmaking and helping someone book the thing, work with them. Finding a car, I imagine is like, I'm not going to just flag down a car. There's challenge there. I'm not going to just go and ask someone, "Can I stay in your home?" There's challenges there.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我想知道你能否举几个糟糕的市场平台创意案例。不过我会总结你刚才提到的三个关键点，我很认同。首先，市场机会在于两端高度碎片化。即双方（用户和服务提供者）都不占据绝对优势，因为如果一方或另一方都是少数巨头，就没必要你来介入了。比如五家航空公司，你不需要市场平台来撮合航空公司。其次，需求统一，基本需求一致。比如我只想住在别人家里，想找辆车带我去某个地方，或者找个水管工。（00:27:04）第三，撮合过程存在障碍，匹配和协助预订服务的复杂性很高。比如找车，我不会随便拦下路过的车。预订民宿也不可能直接上门敲门说：“能住你家吗？”这些都存在挑战。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Are there any examples of companies you've seen that are just like, that will never work as a marketplace, or here's a funny example of a marketplace that tried to be a marketplace and it's not ...
turns.zh: 太棒了。你能否举几个你见过的永远无法成功的市场平台案例，或者一些尝试过却失败的有趣例子？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I don't have a great example of that, but I can give you a tangentially related example of a marketplace that I don't want to throw anyone under the bus. I respect the company and the effort, but Sidecar at the time was another ride-sharing company competing with Lyft and Uber, and there's, I'm sure a whole bunch of lessons there. They ended up closing, but I think one really interesting direction that they took pretty early on to differentiate themselves was, in my mind perhaps very naively a mistake, they decided to give complete control to the user where as a user you had a whole bunch of filters. You could decide, "I want a car that's at least 2015 or newer. I want a driver that's at least this or newer." And so, I think the theory was reasonable on paper. It was like, "Hey, let's give people more control over it." (00:28:29): But you have those other players out there, you have Lyft and Uber, and people feel forced in this standardized experience, "We're going to compete by giving you the choice, you get to decide the experience that you want." I think in reality, it just fragments your marketplace even further, and you have this hyper fragmentation in your marketplace, and I think it hurt their SLAs quite drastically. If you think about the ETA, when you ask explicitly you're like, "Yeah, sure, I want a newer car," and you slide it to 2020 not realizing that you just lost 10 minutes because now we had a great driver, but they have a Honda Civic from 2018, and it's not the special that you wanted. (00:29:08): So, I think people who build marketplaces tend to want to give a lot of control to the users because this is what users want, or this is what comes up oftentimes in user feedback like, "Oh, we have those two distinct group of users. Those ones, they really want new cars. Those ones, they don't want new cars." And so, naturally you have a product team that builds the toggle to get the new cars, and I think the mistake is that you unknowingly fragment your supply in a way that has a much more meaningful impact on the health of your marketplace than you suspect.
turns.zh:
我没有这方面的绝佳案例，但我可以举一个与此相关的例子，虽然不想把任何公司拖下水，但我对这家公司及其努力心怀敬意。Sidecar当时是另一家与Lyft和Uber竞争的网约车公司，我相信其中有很多值得借鉴的经验教训。虽然他们最终倒闭了，但我认为他们早期为实现差异化采取的一个方向——在用户面前赋予完全控制权——或许是个天真之举。用户可以设定诸多筛选条件，比如“我想要2015年或更新的车型”、“我希望司机的车辆至少达到这个年份”。乍一看，这个理念合乎情理——“让我们赋予用户更多自主权，让他们自主选择出行体验”。但现实证明，这种做法只会进一步割裂市场，导致市场过度碎片化，最终严重损害了他们的服务水平协议（SLA）。

以预估到达时间（ETA）为例，当用户明确要求“我想要一辆较新的车型”时，系统可能会把时间拖延到2020年。但用户可能没有意识到，原本有位优秀司机可用，却因为用户坚持要2018款本田思域而错失良机。这暴露出一个关键问题：用户可能希望拥有更多选择权，但这往往会让产品团队陷入两难境地——要么打造满足不同需求的子产品，要么用复杂的切换界面强行满足所有用户。最终，供应链的割裂对市场健康产生了超出预期的负面影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is another awesome example of don't over listen to users and do what you think is going to be best for the business, and this is not even a marketplace lesson. It's just generally you don't want to give users more options than they will need to be successful and happy. And I think Sidecar did that because they were trying to differentiate from Lyft and Uber, like, "What can we do differently?" And they're like, "Oh, let's give people all these options." I think they even let drivers choose the price that they're offering their ride at, which made it extra complicated. They're like, "Oh my God, all these cars at different prices," but I respect their attempt because they were just the third wheel, no pun intended.
turns.zh: 我认为这再次印证了不要过度迎合用户需求、而应坚持商业本位的道理。这甚至不算市场策略的失误，而是产品设计的通病：永远不要给用户超出成功所需的过多选择权。Sidecar之所以走上歧途，是因为他们试图与Lyft和Uber差异化竞争，盲目追随“用户想要新车”的反馈，最终导致供应链崩溃。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Ironically, it's almost the opposite advice that I usually give to companies who struggle with market health, it's if you have different verticals, try if possible to open up your supply walls. Your user is telling you like X, but try to give them something that is tangential to what you think they want, because odds are that they are actually fine with it. There's this amazing example from Thumbtack, it's the smoke machine example. So Thumbtack, now they specialize a little bit more in home services, but a few years ago they were also doing a lot of events. So, you had DJs, you had photographers, and a lot of people were hiring for wedding DJs on the platform. And one of the checkboxes was a smoke machine, and it turns out a lot of people are checking this. You're like, "Yeah, hell yeah, I want a smoke machine at my wedding." (00:31:14): And unknowingly to them, obviously, only 5% of our DJs had a smoke machine, and so you would carve out 95% of our supply. And if when we talked to users, they were like, "Oh, no, no, I don't care that much about the smoke machine. I didn't realize that this was automatically going to remove half of the supply." And so, work on ways to make this checkbox affect the ranking but not the actual filtering is a great example of how you can listen to your users and tweak the experience, but simplify their cognitive load by knowing like, "Hey, we know you prefer a smoke machine, but we're intelligent enough to know it's probably not a deal breaker for you."
turns.zh: 颇具讽刺意味的是，这几乎与我通常给那些在市场健康方面遇到困难的公司提出的建议背道而驰——如果你有多个垂直领域，尽可能开放你的供应壁垒。用户告诉你他们想要X，但你不妨给他们提供与他们预期略有偏差的东西，因为很可能他们对此并无异议。Thumbtack就有一个绝佳的例子——烟雾机案例。Thumbtack现在专注于家居服务，但几年前他们也曾大力开展活动业务。比如，平台上有很多DJ和摄影师在接婚礼DJ的订单，其中一个选项是烟雾机。结果发现，有很多人勾选了这个选项。用户会说：“没错，我婚礼上就想要烟雾机！”（00:31:14）但他们并不知道，平台上只有5%的DJ配备了烟雾机，这意味着95%的供应被排除在外。当我们与用户沟通时，他们会说：“哦，不不，我对烟雾机没那么在意。没想到这会自动筛掉一半的供应。”因此，设计一个让烟雾机选项影响排名而非实际筛选的机制，是一个很好的例子，既能倾听用户需求，又能通过简化认知负荷来提升用户体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that example. The other thing that I think is important to talk about briefly is when you're thinking about building a marketplace, a lot of times they fail because the business model just doesn't work. I think about a company like Cherry that tried to do Uber for car washes, and in theory there's a smart idea of I'm going to just do on-demand car wash. The problem is no one's going to pay what it costs to do that, to a car wash person shows up and washes your car. I think cleaning is another example. There's also just like going-
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个例子。另外，我认为有一点值得简要探讨的是，当你考虑搭建一个市场平台时，很多时候它们会失败，原因在于商业模式本身不行。比如Cherry公司曾尝试为洗车服务打造Uber模式。从理论上讲，按需洗车是个聪明的想法。但问题是，没有人愿意为此支付高昂费用——毕竟洗车师傅上门为你洗车成本太高了。清洁服务也是如此。还有像Exec这样的公司——

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Exec is another one that comes to mind.
turns.zh: Exec？对，就是那种有人上门为你做事的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh Exec, yeah, where it's just like someone come does stuff for you.
turns.zh: 对，某种程度上。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Something, yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And so I guess, is there anything you want to add there? Just like this is another reason your marketplace might fail? And maybe just let me expand on this question. Just what are the most common reasons marketplaces fail in your experience? And I think it's important to say most marketplace ideas fail, just like most startup ideas fail.
turns.zh: 是的。那你还有什么想补充的吗？这也是市场平台可能失败的另一个原因吧？或许我可以进一步展开这个问题。以你经验来看，最常见的市场平台失败原因是什么？我认为大多数市场平台理念都会失败，就像大多数创业项目都会失败一样。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, most ideas period fail, I think. Yes.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得大多数创意都会失败。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Most ideas period fail, same. Coming back to most of the things you're going to struggle with are the same things that every company struggles with outside of marketplace. So, let me just ask, is maybe specifically within marketplaces or even just broadly, what are the biggest reasons that marketplaces fail?
turns.zh: 大多数创意都会失败，道理是一样的。回到你的问题：市场平台面临的难题，往往与非市场平台公司遇到的难题如出一辙。所以我想问，具体到市场平台领域，或者更广泛地说，市场平台失败的最主要原因是什么？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I think a few things come to mind. One is this concept of liquidity that we've talked about. So, you need to kick off this flywheel, you need to build enough of that density within your marketplace. And depending on the business, you can take a lot of time or money, and without the right diagnostic framework you can end up running out of both. And so it's like, that's the same one, and I felt this at Lyft, I've seen this at other companies, this rush like, "Wow, we have to get to this point, otherwise we know it's a losing battle until we have enough density for both sides to have a good enough experience." The other one that I see is ignoring one side. So, we talked about doing that when you're early on, but I see a lot of larger companies operating for too long as one-sided businesses. Many large marketplaces only thinking about their demand side funnel. (00:34:01): So they run ads, they get clicks, they turn those clicks into dollars, and they try to get enough supplies that intuitively the experience is good enough for users. And my advice is, if you're doing this you're missing out on half of your business. And the trick is marketplaces are very laggy, so once your network effects start to die down it turns into this moment of panic of, "Oh shoot, we forgot about half of our users. We forgot that sellers are people too, and they're all leaving, and now we need to completely transform our product to save the ship, and to create a compelling value proposition on their side." So, that's the other thing that I see is businesses realizing that they are marketplaces with true marketplace needs too late in the game. And the last one is quality. I think we talked a little bit about the quality before, but it doesn't mean that you always need to have the best quality in your marketplace, but being a marketplace implies a level of curation. (00:34:58): You need to be intentional about the quality that you aim to provide, and I think a lot of companies don't have necessarily that intentionality and you have this constant push of supply, "If only we'd lower our bar a little bit, we could get more supply." And so until you end up, we've all experienced this at some point, you found some e-commerce website, you look for something and there is also like, "Oh my god, this looks super shady," because all the sellers don't look that great. That's a quality problem. And so, you need to be intentional about your quality and I think that's another area where companies fail.
turns.zh:
我觉得有几点值得深思。首先是我们之前讨论过的流动性概念。也就是说，你需要启动这个增长引擎，在你的市场内积累足够的用户密度。这取决于具体业务，可能需要耗费大量时间和资金，如果没有合理的诊断框架，最终可能会两者皆失。比如说，在Lyft我就深有体会，其他公司也曾遇到过这种情况，急于求成的心态非常明显：“哇，我们必须达到这个阶段，否则在积累足够密度、让双方都能获得优质体验之前，这注定是一场必败之战。”  

另一个问题是忽视一方需求。早期阶段我们谈到过要平衡供需，但我发现很多大公司长期以来都只专注于需求侧的优化。比如，他们投放广告、获取点击量、将点击转化为收益，然后试图通过增加供应来提升用户体验。但我的建议是，如果你只关注这一侧，就会错失一半的市场机遇。关键在于，市场平台的反应非常滞后。一旦网络效应开始减弱，公司就会陷入恐慌：“天哪，我们忽视了半数用户！卖家也是人，他们都在离开，现在我们必须彻底重构产品才能扭转局面，为他们创造有吸引力的价值主张。” 这就是我观察到的另一个痛点——很多公司直到业务后期才意识到自己也是有真实市场需求的平台。  

最后是质量问题。我们之前稍微提过，但这并不意味着你必须追求极致的质量。作为平台，本质上就需要进行内容筛选。（00:34:58）你必须有意识地设定质量标准，但很多公司缺乏这种自觉性，总是想方设法增加供应量：“只要稍微降低门槛，就能吸引更多卖家。” 最终结果往往是用户体验糟糕。比如我们都遇到过这样的电商平台：用户搜索某个商品时，发现卖家信息不靠谱，商品质量堪忧。这就是质量缺失的典型案例。平台需要用心维护质量，这也是很多公司失败的另一个关键点。
