（00:36:23）：延续刚才关于质量的讨论，我想谈谈托管式市场和托管式供应链。市场平台面临质量挑战的核心原因在于：您无法完全掌控供应链，也无法统一管理平台上的供应商——毕竟您并非在销售实体产品，质量管理本质上就是一项挑战。Airbnb不拥有房屋，Uber不雇佣司机。法律上甚至无法明确约束他们的行为，因为这些都是合同工。因此，质量管控始终是市场平台的难题。这推动了市场平台向托管式管理的转型。我们为供应商提供更多指导，或许直接掌控部分供应链，或是大力投入培训等资源。在理想世界中，自主管理的模式能最大限度提升质量。但这种模式会背离市场平台的商业逻辑——毕竟那样的商业模式会失去核心竞争力。对于正考虑加强托管管理的市场平台，您有何建议？何时转向托管模式才合理？又该如何把握尺度？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I think when you're running a marketplace, you tend to sit in your ivory tower a little bit looking at stats and thinking, "If only we could get people to do X, it'd be better for everyone." And I certainly did that in my career. I think that's missing the point that we're humans, and I think sometimes we act in ways that are non-deterministic or intuitive. I'll mention another example, but we'd originally sell leads to pros like plumbers and electricians. And of those leads, obviously only a fraction would turn into actual jobs and revenue for those pros. So, we also saw that those pros were always great at converting leads into jobs. And so, naturally we thought that we could provide a more consistent experience for customers and for pros by improving their ROI and selling bookings directly to those pros. It's a common marketplace move, going from some version of lead to a direct booking. (00:38:22): And digital, great. We knew we were going to improve their ROI by something like 20% maybe, and we launched this and pros hated it. They hated it because they actually subconsciously, they liked the thrill of the sale. They loved this contact with customer, and they sometimes completely overestimated their ability to close the customer. They were like, "You took all those phone calls, they kept me busy. I felt like I was hustling, I was about to close this customer." And so, no matter what the data says of like, "Oh, we increased their earnings by 20%," the pros don't feel this way and it's the right to feel however they want. And we saw the same thing at Lyft when trying to make driver earnings less volatile, we had to fight a lot of that perception and a lot of that peak end effect. So, my call-out here is any attempt at control can be really tricky and backfire in ways that are unpredictable. (00:39:12): You also touched on employment classification. In the U.S., when you talk about controlling supply, all the lawyers are like, "No, no, no, that's not something that we do." Because if you control your supply, then there can be legally classified as employees and be entitled to a whole bunch of benefits. So, my take on this in general is I'm a huge believer, and it really depends on the type of company I should say, obviously, but my take is I'm a huge believer in market forces and empowerment. So, provide guardrails for what a good experience is in your marketplace, set a clear bar for quality, and provide the right coaching and tools for supply to be successful. And then take a step back and see where the gaps are, and invest more in hands-on tactics just to close those gaps more specifically. (00:40:02): So, lots of coaching tools that Lyft, Uber did it, like most marketplaces provide some sort of coaching. You have a review system perhaps, you have stars for your sellers, for sellers who fall below the threshold then coach them, provide them the right tools, the right guidance, what is the standard that you have on your marketplace and help them meet that bar. And for people who fall through the gaps that you have, then that's when you invest in more hands-on tools. And this is one of the things that we did at Lyft also with the rental company that we spent up. I'm happy to tell you more about that, that's interesting.
turns.zh: 我认为，当你运营一个市场平台时，人们往往会坐在象牙塔里，研究数据，然后想：“要是能让用户做成X事，对大家都更有利就好了。” 我自己在职业生涯中也曾这样做过。但我忽视了一个关键点——我们都是人，有时我们的行为会不符合理性预期。比如，我们最初向水管工和电工等专业人士出售客户线索。但这些线索中，只有极少数能真正转化为他们的业务收入。因此，我们发现这些专业人士在将线索转化为实际订单方面非常擅长。于是，我们顺理成章地认为，通过提升他们的投资回报率（ROI）并直接向这些专业人士销售预订服务，能为客户和专业人士提供更一致的体验。这是市场平台常见的转变策略，从某种形式的线索收集到直接预订。（00:38:22）：在数字化领域，我们原本预计ROI能提升约20%，但推行新政策后，专业人士却对此深恶痛绝。他们不满的核心在于，他们潜意识里享受销售过程的刺激，喜欢与客户互动，有时甚至高估了自己成交客户的能力。比如，他们会说：“你接了那么多电话，把我忙得不可开交。我感觉自己在努力促成交易。”尽管数据显示收益增长了20%，但专业人士感受不到这些益处——他们有权按照自己的方式解读现实。Lyft在试图降低司机收入波动时，就遭遇了类似阻力——人们对平台的监管心存戒备，担心这会被法律认定为雇佣关系，从而赋予司机诸多福利。因此，我的核心观点是：任何控制行为都可能适得其反，产生难以预测的负面影响。（00:39:12）：你还提到了就业分类问题。在美国，当谈到控制供应时，律师们会说：“不行，不行，不行，这不是我们的业务。”因为如果控制供应，用户可能被法律认定为雇员，享受一系列福利。因此，我总体上认为——当然，这取决于公司类型——我非常支持市场力量和赋权理念。为市场平台设定优质体验的标准，明确质量门槛，为供应方提供正确的指导和工具，让他们成功运营。然后，退后一步，观察差距，投入更多实际策略来精准填补空白。（00:40:02）：Lyft和Uber等平台都提供了大量辅导工具，比如评分系统、星级评价等。当卖家未达标时，通过指导和工具帮助他们提升。同时，对于表现不佳的卖家，要投入更多实际支持。这也是我们在Lyft与租赁公司合作时采取的策略。很乐意详细分享经验，相信这部分内容很有启发性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to hear about that. Before we hear that, is there any marketplace that has been very good at upleveling quality without becoming managed, that did this really well that you can think of?
turns.zh: 很想听听具体案例。在听之前，有没有哪个市场平台在不进行过度管控的情况下成功提升了质量水平？你能想到的成功案例有哪些？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, there's a talent marketplace called Toptal, and they are specialized in this. They have a really high bar for quality, they claim to only have the top 1%, top 3% I believe, of talent there. And they have a really amazing set of checks and processes. This funny story from them, but apparently they advertise something maybe a 3% pass rate for their talent, so they only on board like 3% of the people who apply. And allegedly their actual pass rate is even lower than that, but they thought that if they actually advertise the actual number it would sound fake. And so, they actually say 3% because 1% would sound like too ridiculous and it would discredit their talent. So, they're one company that does a tremendous amount of work for vetting quality early on with a ton of different checks, but also maintaining that quality. So, throughout with the right coaching tools, with education and things like that.
turns.zh:
是的，有一个叫Toptal的才艺市场，他们专注于这方面业务。他们对人才质量要求极高，我记得他们声称平台上只有最顶尖的1%或3%人才。他们的审核流程和机制也相当严格。听说他们曾宣传人才入选率只有3%，所以实际只招募了约3%的申请者。据说实际通过率甚至更低，但他们觉得如果公布真实数据会显得太离谱，影响人才的公信力。所以他们选择设定3%的标准，因为1%太低会显得不靠谱。

这家公司在人才筛选方面下了很大功夫，通过多重审核机制来保证质量，同时通过培训工具、教育资源等手段维持高水准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good example. And so, basically they just vet and only approve high quality supply in their case. It's mostly engineers, right? I think on Toptal?
turns.zh: 这确实是个很好的例子。基本上，他们会严格筛选，只批准高质量的人才，对吧？我记得Toptal主要招募工程师和设计师吧？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Correct. Yes, it's mostly engineers, designers, I think.
turns.zh: 没错，主要是工程师和设计师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which you can only do if you have so much supply that has so much interest in becoming part of your platform, but that's a really cool example. Basically it's just only allow really high quality supply. Let's hear this rental car story, so this is Lyft trying to do rental cars, right?
turns.zh: 但这只有在你有大量高素质人才且他们对加入平台有浓厚兴趣的情况下才能做到。不过Toptal的例子确实很值得借鉴。他们的做法就是只允许高质量的人才入驻。接下来听听Lyft进军租车业务的故事吧？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Correct. Yes, yes. Yeah, so this is a little bit of context. I was leading the driver's side of product at Lyft, and General Motors had invested half a billion dollars in our last round of funding. And this was Christmas Eve, I'll always remember, I got a call from Lyft CEO and General Motors CTO, and we decided to build a rental company essentially. And the reason for it was really fascinating. GM had all those vehicles that were coming off of lease, and that they were forced to sell at auctions they didn't really know what to do with. And from our perspective, we had this massive supply gap. We've talked about this before, but we had this huge supply crunch, we were growing super fast and couldn't hire drivers fast enough, couldn't onboard drivers fast enough. And when we looked at the market, we realized that 50% of the job seekers and welfare recipients in the U.S. don't have a car. (00:43:26): So, that was our supply gap. This was a huge pool of people that we just couldn't tap into because they didn't have a car. And so, by renting cars we could essentially manufacture our own supply. We could dial this up and down, we could be very surgical about how many vehicles do we bring in, which markets do we bring this in, at what price? We could even offer to pay for the car if they drove 30 hours a week and completely transform the lives of those people, now we allow them to have true mobility. They can go buy groceries, they can go take the kids on vacation. So, a huge win-win for everybody with something like this. And I think in few months we had built a rental company from the ground up, and within 18 months I think we were the fourth-largest rental fleet in the U.S. (00:44:10): But all of this stemmed from this gap that we saw of like, okay, it's not about controlling the drivers in general. It's about like, okay, we want to be surgical. We want to control the quality of the cars on the platform. So, we talked about that, that's a great example. In the markets where we thought the vehicles of quality was too low, we knew we could onboard more rental vehicles that were more recent to raise the average age of a vehicle on the platform. So, it gave us more control in a much more surgical way, I guess.
turns.zh: 没错。是的，是的。好的，我先讲点背景。我在Lyft负责司机端产品，当时通用汽车在我们上一轮融资中投资了5亿美元。圣诞前夜，我永远记得接到Lyft首席执行官和通用汽车首席技术官的电话，我们决定建立一家租车公司。原因其实很吸引人。通用汽车有很多即将退租的车辆，这些车被迫在拍卖会上出售，但他们不知道如何处理。从我们的角度来看，我们面临着巨大的供应缺口。我们之前谈过这个问题——供应严重不足，公司发展速度极快，但司机招募速度跟不上。再看市场数据，美国50%的求职者和领取福利金的人没有车。（00:43:26）这就是我们的供应缺口。这是一大批潜在客户群体，因为他们没有车而无法利用。我们通过租车业务可以自主控制供应规模，精准调整投放节奏，选择合适的市场和定价策略。比如，如果司机每周开车30小时以上，我们甚至可以承担租车费用，彻底改变他们的生活。现在他们可以去买菜、带孩子度假。这对各方来说都是双赢。几个月内，我们从零开始搭建了租车业务，18个月内就成为美国第四大租车公司。（00:44:10）但这一切都源于我们发现的缺口。关键不在于全面控制司机，而是要精准把控平台车辆的质量。我们针对车辆质量不达标的市场，引入更新的租赁车辆，提高平台车辆的平均车龄。这让我们能更有效地控制质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, it's not that you are launching a rental car service, the idea was add supply and give drivers a car so that they could become drivers.
turns.zh: 所以这不是要推出租车服务，而是要增加供应，为司机提供车辆，让他们成为职业司机。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: It was a bit of both. We actually launched, it was we had vehicles that drivers could rent from Lyft, and to drive on the platform, and also to drive for their personal needs essentially. But yeah.
turns.zh: 两者兼而有之。实际上，我们推出了两项服务：一是司机可以在Lyft平台上租用车辆用于接单，二是司机可以租车用于个人出行。但确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it, okay. And then, did this actually work and have impact? Was this a good idea?
turns.zh: 明白了。那这个策略是否成功了？是否产生了实际影响？这是个好主意吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, it had a tremendous impact. Like I mentioned, I think we scaled this exponentially to become, I think again, the fourth-largest rental fleet in the U.S. because it was so effective for us, both because we had the right amount of control, but also those drivers were incredibly loyal to us. We had a whole bunch of other incentives that we could do, we could offer to pay for the car but only if you don't drive for the competition for Uber, and only if you drive at least 30 hours a week. So, this again provided us with, again, much greater retention, much higher engagement, and was a real incentive for us but also for the drivers.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，效果非常显著。正如我提到的，我们以指数级速度扩展业务，成为美国第四大租车公司，因为这个策略对我们非常有效。一方面我们实现了精准控制，另一方面这些司机对我们也非常忠诚。我们还设计了其他激励措施，比如只为在Lyft平台上接单的司机支付租车费用，但条件是每周至少开车30小时。这些举措进一步提高了留存率和用户参与度，对我们和司机都是双赢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And maybe the reason it's most interesting is this is along the spectrum of a managed marketplace. It moves closer to you guys are paying and covering costs of cars. It makes it less just like this simple, highly efficient marketplace.
turns.zh: 太棒了。或许最有趣的是，这与管理型市场的理念不谋而合。它正朝着让用户承担汽车费用的方向发展，而非仅仅停留在一个简单、高效的市场层面。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. It's the marketplace version of maybe your black car fleet owner has their fleet of vehicle and they have people. So, this was the marketplace version of doing that.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。这就好比黑车车队的老板们把车队管理权交给专业机构，然后雇人打理车辆。这种模式本质上就是市场化运作的典范。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's also just a differentiator, because GM and you guys were close, and so you had this lever that say Uber didn't have. Amazing. Another area that I know you spent time on that I think is really interesting, and I think it'd be helpful to people to hear is the mentorship program, and the ambassador program that you had at Lyft, and how that helped you scale much more quickly than other folks were able to. Can you share that story?
turns.zh: 这也是一个关键的差异化因素，因为通用汽车和你们的关系本来就很密切，所以你们掌握了优步所不具备的竞争优势。太厉害了。我知道你们在另一个领域也下了不少功夫，我觉得这部分内容对听众很有启发——就是Lyft推行的导师计划和大使计划。这些举措如何帮助你们比其他公司更快地实现规模扩张？能跟我们分享一下相关故事吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Pretty early on at Lyft, this was 2014, 2015 maybe, Uber was basically 30X our size. They had 30 times more revenue, more people, more liquidity, everything you can think of. They were growing like crazy, and we had a bit of this existential moment, as you can imagine, where we were wondering how we're supposed to compete with that. And we had to be super clever, everything that you did at the company had to be 10 times more efficient per person than the competition just to survive. That was the bar, just not to die, and put a lot of pressure on us but we basically found a clever way of onboarding drivers at a fraction of the cost and resources. So, let me give you a little bit of context on how the onboarding flow worked. So, at the time, the last step to get onboarded as a driver was after you background check and your driving record check came back, you had to do a visual inspection of your car, a quick test drive, some light training, and we would check your documents. (00:47:53): We would check that you are the person with a driver's license and all those things. And Uber at the time would launch a team on the ground, they would go and open an office and they would have DMV-style group onboarding sessions and car inspections. And we did this as well in our first three to four markets, but you can imagine the overhead and the lead time. You had to go and you had to find office space, sign the lease, hire employees, you had huge, huge lead time. And we thought about it, and at the time a huge competitive differentiator for us was our brand. As a passenger or as a driver, why would you use a platform with lower liquidity? As a driver, you had lower earnings guaranteed. As a passenger, you had longer wait times. Why would you use a service like that? You do because of the brand, because of its values, it's how it makes you feel. (00:48:41): And so, we had the pink mustaches at the time, we had this very strong brand identity. I think a lot of that has been lost now, but we also had this amazing community of drivers who were fierce advocates for the brand. And so, what we did is leveraging this community and building essentially a soft onboarding supply engine where we would pay our best drivers $35 per mentor session, and a mentor session was essentially replacing this onboarding flow. So, it was basically another driver looking at your vehicle to check all your documents, take photos of your driver's license and all that stuff, and take you on a short ride along. And the benefits of this were absolutely mind-blowing and kind of unexpected for us on all sides. First, the mentors were our very best drivers, and they were evangelists for the brand. So, what they did was they would share personal tips on when and where to drive. (00:49:34): Oftentimes they shared their contact info. And this created tremendous leverage and social proof for those new drivers who were on the fence about taking strangers into their car. It's actually quite funny because we had the brightest minds in the company writing the best marketing emails and copy, like, "Hey, hop on the car and drive this Saturday." And you had all those drivers and all those mentors like, "No, no, don't listen to those Lyft guys. Here's what you should do. Go on Tuesday at 2:00 PM, text me, I'll tell you where the good spot is, and this is how you're going to get rides. This is how you're going to get rich and make a lot of money." And this recognition lever was just so much more powerful than anything we could be telling you. And so, very, very efficient activation lever for the new drivers. For us, also incredibly scalable. (00:50:22): We could fly a small team to rigorously vet and onboard maybe like 10, 20 top drivers, and then they'd fly to a different market, and we would let the rest of our drivers be onboarded by those mentors. And even for those mentors, for those top drivers, it was an incredible recognition lever. For them, if you were a 4.9 driver, you had enough rides, you had a chance to make it into being a mentor, and this provided additional earnings opportunity for you. If you did two mentor sessions in an hour, you could make 70 bucks an hour. You could take a break from driving if you're tired, and just do some of those. It felt like getting promoted at a job. And so, it actually had a huge impact on the retention of our very best drivers, which was unexpected. So, a lot of really, really interesting benefits, and we actually lean into this and built a couple of really fascinating variations of this for a while, but this allowed us to match most of Uber's footprint with a 10th or a 20th of the resources at incredible speed, I guess.
turns.zh:
早在Lyft成立之初，大约是2014年或2015年的时候，Uber的规模比我们大30倍。他们拥有30倍于我们的营收、更多员工、更充足的流动资金，以及你能想到的所有优势。他们发展势头迅猛，而我们当时也面临着一个生死存亡的关键时刻——要如何与Uber竞争？我们必须想尽办法做到高效。公司里的每一项决策都要比竞争对手高效十倍，才能在激烈的竞争中生存下来。

让我来解释一下司机注册流程的具体细节。当时流程的最后一步是，在背景调查和驾驶记录审核通过后，司机需要接受车辆检查、快速试驾、简短培训，并提交相关文件。（00:47:53）我们会核实他们的驾照信息等资质。而Uber当时则派遣地面团队开设办公室，进行类似车管所的批量注册和车辆检查。我们在最初的三到四个市场也采用了这种模式，但成本和周期实在太高——需要租赁办公场地、签署租约、招聘员工，耗时巨大。我们深思熟后，意识到品牌是我们最大的竞争优势。无论是乘客还是司机，都会选择流动性更高的平台。司机能获得更高的收益保障，乘客则能享受更短的等待时间。（00:48:41）基于此，我们打造了粉色胡子标志的品牌标识，凝聚了强大的社区力量。如今这些元素或许已被淡化，但当时司机们是品牌的忠实拥护者。我们的策略是借助这个社区，构建柔性化的注册流程——让优秀司机担任导师，每次指导收费35美元。导师不仅检查车辆、拍照留存，还会亲自带新司机试驾。这种模式带来的效益令人惊叹：

首先，导师都是我们的顶级司机，他们是品牌的传播者。他们会分享最佳驾驶时间和地点，甚至主动提供联系方式。这为新司机消除了对陌生人的信任顾虑。最有趣的是，公司最聪明的团队写的营销邮件常是：“周六快来开车吧。”而导师们却说：“别听Lyft那帮人的！周二下午两点来，我告诉你哪里好赚。”这种口口相传的认可效果远超任何宣传攻势，成为最有效的激活工具。
新的司机团队。对我们而言，这套体系还具备极强的可扩展性。（00:50:22）我们可以派遣一支小团队，对约10到20名顶级司机进行严格筛选和培训，然后让这些司机前往其他市场，为我们剩余的司机提供入职指导。即便对这些顶级司机而言，这也是一种极好的认可机制。只要你的评分达到4.9分（满分5.0），完成足够多的订单，就有机会晋升为导师。这为他们提供了额外的收入来源——如果每小时进行两场导师培训，时薪最高可达70美元。疲惫时可以暂停开车专心指导，整个过程就像职场晋升一样。令人意外的是，这套机制对保留最优秀司机的效果显著。通过这种方式，我们仅用Uber十分之一或二十分之一的资源成本，就能以极快的速度复制其大部分业务版图。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing story, and it's such a great lever that I totally agree, I don't hear people using and I wonder why. So, what I'm hearing is it was cheaper, the drivers were making money. I imagine the drivers trained by the mentors ended up being better drivers, that's what we saw at Airbnb, hosts that came in through a referral ended up being better hosts, for whatever reason. And you're saying basically, this is what allowed you to compete with Uber at a much smaller scale and much less money raised. Amazing.
turns.zh: 真是个精彩的故事！这确实是个绝佳的策略，我完全赞同，可惜没听过别人用过，不知道为什么。听你讲，成本更低了，司机们也能赚到钱。我想，经过导师培训的司机最终会成为更优秀的司机——正如我们在Airbnb看到的，通过推荐加入的房东最终也表现得更出色。不管出于什么原因，你的意思是，这让你们能以更小的规模、更少的资金与Uber竞争，真是了不起。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said there's a couple of variations. Is there anything interesting there to share, just things that you built as a follow-up based on the success?
turns.zh: 你说还有几个变体。能分享些有趣的案例吗？比如基于成功经验开发的后续产品？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: So, the next step in that journey was basically we were growing like crazy, but now we had cracks in like the activation phase, but now we had a whole bunch of people dropping off in the funnel before activation]. So, they didn't enter their SSN, they didn't enter the right info for us to run all those checks in the previous steps of the onboarding flow. So, we built a team of hundreds of account executives, and their job was just pick up the phone and call those drivers. And so, we had the same aha moment of like could we get some of our best drivers to do that for us, and empower them to be a part of this? And so, we did this and we launched another, like I said, role. We called them recruiters. And so, as a recruiter, as a driver, you could just, if this was quiet on the road, you could just hop on your phone and you would have a mini sales dashboard where you could claim leads. (00:52:49): And this was a driver who had dropped off in the funnel, and you had a telephone number, you could just call them and text them. And same thing, those guys were outperforming our very best of trained salespeople, because it's not like, "Hey, it's Ben from Lyft. Hop on the road, please." It's like, "Hey, my name is James and I'm a fellow driver as well. Lyft told me that you have a incomplete application. Do you have any questions? Do you want me to come to your house, we can do this together?" And we would pay them 20 bucks per person that they converted to activation. And so, something incredibly scalable for us, another way for us to reward and recognize our best drivers. (00:53:27): And it also provided a really interesting way for us to smooth out the supply and demand. The problem with a marketplace like Lyft is that you have this big spike. Everyone wants to drive on a Tuesday at 2:00 PM, but everyone wants rides on a Saturday at 2:00 AM. And so, how can you manufacture demand during those low utilization times? This was a great way to do that. Now you could wait on the road and still make money while just sitting in your car while waiting for the next ride. So, this was another iteration of this model that was really cool.
turns.zh: 接下来的挑战是，用户增长速度惊人，但激活阶段出现了漏洞——大量用户在激活前就流失了。比如他们没填写社会安全号码，或者信息不全导致后续审核失败。于是我们组建了数百人的客户经理团队，让他们直接打电话联系司机。后来我们又有了灵光一闪的想法：能否让优秀司机加入这个团队？于是我们推出了新角色——招募专员。作为招募专员，司机只需在空闲时拿起手机，查看潜在客户信息，进行电话沟通。（00:52:49）这类用户通常在激活流程中流失，我们会提供电话号码，鼓励他们主动联系。结果这些司机的表现远超专业销售团队，因为不是那种生硬的推销：“我是Lyft的本，请上路吧。”而是亲切地说：“我是詹姆斯，也是司机。Lyft提示你申请不完整，有什么问题吗？我可以上门帮你填。”成功激活一个用户就能获得20美元奖励。这对我们来说是可扩展的模式，也是奖励优秀司机的创新方式。（00:53:27）它还巧妙地平衡了供需矛盾。Lyft这样的平台存在高峰低谷问题，比如周二下午2点大家都想开车，但周六凌晨2点却无人叫车。如何在低谷期创造需求？这个模式完美解决了这个问题——司机可以在路上等待，同时通过接单赚钱。真是绝妙的迭代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That is so cool. I just know the feeling of being on a team, coming up with this idea and the thing working must feel so great. Just like, "Holy shit, look at this. Look at all these cool things that we can do with our supply." Something I wasn't going to get into, but it might be interesting just to hear if you have thoughts on this. So, I've been a huge fan of Lyft from the beginning, I used Lyft the very first weekend it came out in San Francisco when there was like five drivers. It was like a beta test, I was friends with someone that worked at Lyft early on, and it was just like, "Man, Lyft's the best." I was like all Lyft, Uber sucks, I hate that. I want to give it the fist bump or the mustache. So great. Today though, I was just looking at market caps. (00:54:38): So, Uber is worth $150 billion, Lyft is worth $5 billion. I'm curious if you have thoughts on just, it feels like Uber has won at this point, and I don't know where Lyft goes. I know your heart is with Lyft and you worked at Lyft for a long time, I know it doesn't feel great to see how things have played out necessarily. I'm curious just to hear your take on just what do you think Uber did, if you look back, that allowed them to basically win? And where do you think Lyft goes from here? What do you think happens with Lyft? They're still worth 5 billion, it's still a huge, amazing, successful business, but just where do you think things go?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是太酷了。我深知团队协作的感觉——构思出一个点子，然后看着它成功运作，这种感觉一定无与伦比。就像"天哪，看看这个。看看我们用现有资源能做出的这些超酷玩意儿！"虽然我本不打算深入探讨，但听听你的看法或许会很有意思。我从一开始就是Lyft的忠实粉丝。旧金山Lyft刚上线那个周末，我就在用，当时司机才五个左右。感觉就像在参加测试版测试。我早期认识Lyft的一位员工朋友，当时就觉得"天哪，Lyft简直太棒了！"我当时对Lyft赞不绝口，嫌弃Uber糟糕透顶，恨不得为Lyft击掌或者竖起大拇指。太棒了。不过今天我刚看了市值数据。（00:54:38）Uber市值1500亿美元，Lyft只有50亿美元。我很好奇你对此怎么看。感觉Uber现在已经胜出了，而Lyft的未来走向尚不明朗。我知道你对Lyft情有独钟，在那里工作了很久，看到现在局面肯定心里不舒服。我想听听你对Uber成功的关键因素有什么见解，以及你对Lyft未来发展的看法。Lyft市值50亿美元，虽然仍然是一家庞大、成功的企业，但你觉得它接下来的路会怎么走？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah. I think it all went south when I left the company. I'm just kidding. No, and again, I have to call out the fact that I haven't been close to Lyft, and their business and strategy for many years at this point. So, take this with a grain of salt. This is my very naive perspective, but I think to me, perhaps the biggest blow to Lyft's business was somewhat inherent, like the vision. Lyft's vision was always anchored around transportation, people of transportation. The founders were deeply passionate about moving people, they were passionate about transforming the way people move around in a city. They wanted to just change how cities are designed, how roads are designed. And so, that meant investing in dynamic shuttles and things like that, and there's a lot of experimentation that went to that. But it also meant that Lyft never invested in things like food delivery, or goods and parcels, and things like that. (00:56:26): And I think that crushed them during COVID essentially. I think Uber had, I think at some point their slogan was moving in bits and atoms, or something like that. But I think it implies this notion of being a logistics platform for assets in the world, for transporting people, for transporting things, for transporting ... And I think they built, they invested lot in trucks and food delivery, and all those really exotic things that Lyft had never any intention to invest in. Not even because of the lack of resources, but because this was in part a distraction from our vision. We wanted to change how people move around in cities, we wanted to reinvent public transportation, we did not want to be a DoorDash competitor and help you get in donuts during COVID. And a huge part of it also was leaning heavily in shared rides. And so, this was like, again, how do you reinvent public transportation? (00:57:28): It's like every car is a dynamic bus, and now there's a bus line. The bus line is always running, it's always by your house. So, a lot of our investment I think in thinking went in that direction, and the last thing that people wanted with COVID was to be in a car with five strangers, but what people wanted is food delivered to their house. And so, I know that the business had a huge blow during COVID, whereas I think Uber was able to rebound much more quickly because of how diversified the business was. And so, it's funny now because I think Lyft actually killed shared rides, which was just so core to their identity. They were the first ones to launch this. And so yeah, the new COO I think killed the shared rides, which actually I'm really sad about. But yeah, so I think it indicates a very different vision now, a very different direction for the business. And yeah, that's my take, I guess.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得我离开公司后，情况就一落千丈了。不过说笑的，不说这个了。说真的，我已经好多年没怎么关注Lyft及其业务战略了，所以大家听我说这番话时请别太当真。这只是我个人的粗浅看法。在我看来，Lyft业务最大的挫折或许源于其愿景存在固有缺陷。Lyft的愿景始终围绕交通展开，核心是交通服务。创始人们对移动人群充满热情，致力于改变城市交通方式，甚至想重新设计城市布局和道路结构。因此，他们投入大量资源开发动态拼车服务，并进行了诸多相关探索。但这也导致Lyft从未涉足外卖配送、货运物流等领域。（00:56:26）这在新冠疫情期间给他们带来了致命打击。Uber曾宣扬“以原子和比特为单位移动资源”的口号，暗示其目标是成为全球资产物流平台——无论是人员运输、货物配送还是其他服务。但Uber却在卡车运输、外卖配送等奇特领域大举投资，而这些业务与Lyft的初衷背道而驰。不仅因为资源匮乏，更重要的是这些偏离了核心愿景。我们想改变城市交通模式，重塑公共交通体系，而不是在疫情期间充当DoorDash的竞争对手帮用户买甜甜圈。Lyft还过度依赖拼车业务，试图以此革新公共交通。（00:57:28）但这其实是南辕北辙——每辆车都成了动态公交车，现在公交线路无处不在。但疫情期间人们最不需要的是与五个陌生人共乘一车，而最需要的是送货上门服务。显然，疫情对Lyft造成了毁灭性打击，而Uber因业务多元化得以快速复苏。这挺有趣的，因为Lyft自己亲手毁掉了拼车业务——而这本是其核心特色。首位COO接手后就取消了拼车服务，这让我深感遗憾。不过这也表明如今Lyft的愿景与发展方向已然迥异。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So, essentially COVID really effed them because their strategy was always about transportation, and when nobody needs a ride and people want food, strategically Uber made a really good move expanding into food delivery, which I think was a bigger business than rides for a long time. I don't know where it's at today for Uber, and Lyft didn't have that, and it's hard to recover from a time like that. So, it sounds like it's a combination of strategy was pointing Lyft in a certain direction, and circumstances in the world just made it really hard-
turns.zh: 有意思。所以说新冠疫情确实把他们搞砸了，因为他们的战略始终围绕交通展开，而当没人需要打车、人们只想买外卖时，Uber扩展到外卖配送领域的策略堪称妙招，我觉得这项业务长期来说比打车业务规模更大。我不知道Uber如今的情况如何，但Lyft没有抓住这个机会，在那样的时期想翻盘确实难上加难。所以看来，战略方向与外部环境的双重夹击让Lyft陷入困境——

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: And losing me me.
turns.zh: 我也听不懂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And losing Ben. So, you left in 2019, March 2019, and is that when they went public?
turns.zh: 还有失去本。所以，你在2019年3月离开的，那时他们上市了吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Not for the IPO.
turns.zh: 不是因为IPO。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and it's all downhill from then. And then-
turns.zh: 是啊，从那以后一切都走下坡路了。然后——

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I'm telling you.
turns.zh: 我跟你说。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... during COVID actually, when there was a big bump, which I think when people started riding again, and then it went down again. So, I think there was a correlation there, so there we go. That's the thing, don't ever fire Ben, don't let Ben leave. That's our take on it.
turns.zh: ……实际上是在新冠疫情期间，当时市场出现大幅波动。我觉得等人们重新开始交易后，情况又恶化了。所以，我觉得这两者之间有联系，明白了。关键是，千万别解雇本，别让他离开。这就是我们的看法。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I was not fired, yeah. Just to be clear.
turns.zh: 我不是被解雇的，对了。先说清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, just different ways you might leave a company, don't let it happen.
turns.zh: 好的，只是离开公司的方式不同，别让这种情况发生。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I know, I'm kidding.
turns.zh: 我知道，我开玩笑的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so there's two more things I want to spend a little time on before we close up. One is your work in Europe, so you're a product leader in Europe, and I want to hear a little bit about what it's like to be a product person in Europe. And then two, I want to hear about the startup. So, at this point no one can actually fire. You have your own company that you're running, and I want to spend a little time here. Usually we don't spend time on this sort of stuff, but you're working on something very cool that I think is going to be really helpful to a lot of people in a really meaningful way. So, I want to spend a little time there. But before that, so you're living in France now. Before you started your company, you were interviewing for CPR roles in France, you work with a lot of French companies, European companies. I'm curious what you've noticed might be different in the cultures of tech companies in France and Europe in general versus the U.S.
turns.zh: 好的，在结束前，我还想再花点时间谈两件事。一是你的欧洲工作经历，你在欧洲担任产品负责人，想听听在欧洲做产品经理的感受。二是创业公司的情况。目前没人能真正解雇你了，你自己经营着公司，想聊聊这部分。通常我们不常谈这些，但你的项目很酷，我觉得会对很多人有很大帮助。先说你现在住在法国。在创办公司前，你在法国面试CPR职位，还和很多法国公司、欧洲公司合作过。想了解法国和欧洲的科技公司文化与美国相比有什么不同。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: It's been really fascinating, I think. So, my entire career has been in the U.S., and I'm just starting to understand what that European and the French market in particular looks like. And my read so far is that product management has really exploded I think in Europe in recent years, but the market dynamics are still quite different. In the U.S. I think you have this inherently very liquid and dynamic market. I think, this is my interpretation of it, but I think it leads to greater ownership and accountability for people and product at all levels. So, product managers and leaders, they join a startup and you're immediately in charge of a relatively meaningful piece of the business, with genuine autonomy oftentimes. It doesn't always happen, but oftentimes I think that's the case. And if things don't work out, well, there's this expectation that you'll be managed out. (01:01:09): There are countless memes on LinkedIn about the tenure of CPOs at tech companies to illustrate that. I think in France the market is much less liquid, so it's incredibly difficult to change jobs, and it's very expensive to fire someone in France. So, it seems to lead to two effects beyond the obvious job security. One is, I think PMs tend to have less autonomy and ownership, and a little bit more like micromanagement. And there are also less business owners than they can be in the U.S. And I see founders and managers struggling to let go of control a little bit more, again because it's understandable in a way, you don't have as much of a control as you do in the U.S. And so, you see a lot of really fascinating effects. (01:01:55): You have startups who tend to wait a little bit longer before hiring, especially in product. The art of product a little bit less of a thing. You have a lot of amazing PMs in France, but the recognition of the craft is a little bit different outside of the people who practice it. And you have a lot of real interesting outsourcing also, you see startups and companies of all sizes actually relying on great product studios, like Mozza, to build end-to-end products from the ground up. So, something that's been really, really interesting. Another side that I see is this dominance of business over tech in France. (01:02:35): There isn't as much of a cult of technology and software engineering in France as there is in the U.S. And so, the French Ivy League schools are business schools, like HEC, and the most highly valuable skill that you get is soft skills around management and business. It differs from the stereotype of the CS degree, Stanford dropout that you have in Silicon Valley. And I think because of a few of those things that I just mentioned, less liquid job market, but also less liquid financial markets, the last thing that I've observed that's interesting that's also around ownership I guess, is equity is much less meaningful in France. So, of the product leaders that I talked to, most of them consider their equity to be virtually worthless. None of them know of anyone who's made a down payment on a house thanks to their sort of equity. (01:03:25): So, it's seen as a nice bonus, but it's not the token of ownership and the promise of future wealth that it can be in the U.S. when you join a startup. For exec roles, I think it's often sub 10% of their total compensation, whereas in the U.S. it's very often more than 50% of your compensation will be equity. So, that's been interesting in terms of the dynamic, but it's also been real interesting to just see how vibrant the startup culture is here in France. You have a truly exciting innovation happening, especially in AI. You have a lot of French companies at the forefront of this, like Mistral AI and Hugging Face, and things like that. (01:04:03): And also how it's been exciting to see how the government is leaning into that as a catalyst for this innovation. I think the French government has dedicated something like $2.5 billion in funding to support French AI excellence by 2030. So, they're running a lot of internal government incubators to try to disrupt some of the government functions from the inside, and they're hiring top talents to do that. I've met some of the people working on this, it's just really fascinating. It makes me super excited about what a federal startup task of reinventing [inaudible 01:04:38] would look like. So yeah, it's been really exciting to see the whole space and how it differs from the U.S.
turns.zh:
这一切真的非常有趣。我在美国度过了整个职业生涯，现在才开始了解欧洲市场，尤其是法国市场的情况。根据我目前的观察，近年来欧洲的产品管理领域确实蓬勃发展，但市场动态仍有很大不同。在美国，我认为市场本质上极具流动性和活力。我对此的理解是，这导致各级人员对产品拥有更大的自主权和责任感。所以，产品经理和领导者加入初创公司后，往往能立即负责业务的关键部分，通常享有真正的自主权。当然，这种情况并非普遍存在，但确实存在不少这样的例子。若项目失败，公司往往会自然淘汰相关人员。（01:01:09）：领英上无数关于科技公司首席产品官任期的梗图，生动地说明了这一点。在法国，市场流动性要低得多，跳槽困难重重，裁员成本高昂。因此，除了显而易见的就业保障问题外，还会产生两个影响。其一，产品经理的自主权往往较低，微观管理现象更为常见。与美国相比，法国拥有产品负责人的数量更少。创业者和管理者往往难以放权，这在某种程度上是可以理解的，毕竟他们无法像在美国那样完全掌控局面。由此产生了许多有趣的现象。（01:01:55）：初创公司往往更愿意延迟招聘产品人员，产品管理艺术在法国的重要性有所降低。虽然法国也有很多优秀的产品经理，但除非是业内从业者，否则对这一职业的认可度较低。此外，外包现象也十分普遍，许多初创公司和大企业会依赖Mozza等专业产品工作室，从零开发端到端产品。这确实非常引人注目。另一个观察点是法国商业对科技的支配地位。（01:02:35）：法国不像美国那样存在对技术和软件工程的狂热崇拜。法国的常春藤盟校都是商学院，比如HEC，培养的核心技能是管理和商业软技能，这与硅谷那些计算机科学学位、斯坦福辍学者的刻板印象截然不同。基于上述种种因素——市场流动性低、金融市场不活跃——我注意到法国股权的价值远低于美国。在我接触的产品负责人们中，大多数认为自己的股权几乎一文不值，没有人听说过有谁靠股权首付买房。（01:03:25）：在法国，股权被视为不错的福利，但远非美国初创公司中股权所承载的所有权象征和未来财富承诺。对于高管职位，股权通常占总薪酬的不到10%，而在美国，高管薪酬中股权往往占50%以上。这些差异既有趣又发人深省，同时也让我深刻体会到法国初创文化的蓬勃生机。
令人兴奋的创新正在发生，尤其是在人工智能领域。法国有很多处于这一领域前沿的公司，比如Mistral AI和Hugging Face等。（01:04:03）看到政府大力推动这项创新，助力行业发展，也令人振奋。我了解到，法国政府计划到2030年投入约25亿美元资金，支持法国在人工智能领域的卓越发展。此外，政府还设立了多个内部孵化器，试图从内部颠覆一些政府职能，并为此招募顶尖人才。我曾与参与这些项目的人员交流过，这一切都令人着迷。这让我对联邦政府若开展重塑某个领域的创业任务会呈现怎样的局面充满期待。总之，见证这一创新生态的蓬勃发展，以及它与美国市场的差异，实在令人振奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. So, I know there's also AI regulation that feels really strange in Europe, but think that's EU based, not like France specifically.
turns.zh: 真有意思。所以，我知道欧洲的AI监管也让人觉得很奇怪，但我觉得这主要是欧盟层面的，而不是法国特有的。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that people are not excited about. There's just a lot of fear of AI, and so there's a lot of regulation talk in Europe.
turns.zh: 是啊，大家对AI都挺担忧的，因此欧洲有很多监管讨论。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I'm a big Android guy, and a lot of the features like Gemini and all this is only available in the U.S., and now that I'm in France I see the difference a little bit.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢安卓系统，但很多功能比如Gemini之类的，只有在美国才能用，现在我在法国，稍微能感受到些差别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So, the cultural differences you spoke of, do you think they're rooted in the fact that people don't move jobs often, or is it culture? People just don't learn to work in the way that people learn to work in the U.S. in the product role? What do you think is the root of why things are so different?
turns.zh: 有意思。你说的文化差异，你觉得是因为人们不常换工作吗？还是文化原因？人们不习惯按照美国产品角色的工作方式来工作？你觉得为什么会有这么大的差异？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: I'm not quite sure, it's a good question. My take, and I think this is I'm sure very naive and reductive, and I know this is one of my core principles, so I'm sure I also have a tunnel vision on this a little bit. But to me, one of the biggest difference that I see is really around this concept of ownership and accountability. Whereas in the U.S., and again, I saw it, I'm sure you saw it at Airbnb, you see it at a lot of companies, not everywhere, but a lot of companies will hire you, give you a big chunk of the business, and it's up to you to prove yourself out. Where you have six months, you have a year, it's up to you to show impact. I think the French employment model is less conducive to this type of dynamic, because employment is much more rigid. (01:06:20): So, you have much less of this hire now and prove yourself out, it's much more of prove yourself beforehand. And if you've made a bad hire than as a founder, you become perhaps a little bit cagey about your vision. You want to be more hands-on because you made a bad hire. It's not like someone perfect, then he'll make you work but it means you'll be more hands-on in the work of PMs daily, and perhaps we'll think like, "Oh, maybe I don't need product managers who want on my vision, I'll hire project managers," or something like that. So, it's perhaps slightly more conducive to those types of dynamics.
turns.zh: 我不太确定，这是个很好的问题。我的看法——我知道这可能很天真、很简化——但这确实是我的核心观点之一，所以我可能在这方面有些片面。但在我看来，最大的差异在于所有权和责任感的概念。在美国，我见过这种情况，我相信你在Airbnb也见过，很多公司不都是先雇人，然后给你一大块业务，让你自己证明自己吗？比如说六个月、一年时间证明自己。我觉得法国雇佣模式不太利于这种动态，因为雇佣关系太僵化了。（01:06:20）所以，这里没有那么多先雇人再证明自己的情况，而是先证明自己再雇人。如果雇错了人，作为创始人，你可能就会对自己的愿景变得谨慎。你会更亲力亲为，因为你雇错了人。不是说必须要完美的人，然后让他们工作，而是意味着你会更亲力亲为地管理PM们的日常工作，也许我们会想，“哦，也许我不需要认同我愿景的产品经理，我还是雇项目经理吧。”所以，这可能更利于那种动态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're saying that's in part because it's harder to fire people in France and in Europe?
turns.zh: 你说这部分是因为法国和欧洲解雇员工更难？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, I think so. It's not just about firing I think, to be clear, I just think it's culturally the market seems like a lot less liquid and dynamic.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得是这样。说实话，不只是解雇的问题，我只是觉得文化上，市场似乎没那么灵活、没那么活力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, people don't move around as much, they stick around for a long time.
turns.zh: 所以，人们不怎么跳槽，待的时间很长。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. And it sounds like there's also just a cultural difference of founders innately are much more, "I am in control, and I'm not going to hire people and trust you to take this thing on. I'm just going to run the show." It's basically Paul Graham's founder mode is already instilled in everyone.
turns.zh: 明白了。听起来还有一个文化差异，就是创始人天生更倾向于“我要掌控一切，我不会雇人然后信任他们去接手这件事。我要亲自把控一切。”基本上保罗·格雷厄姆的创始人模式已经深深印在每个人心中了。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Maybe yeah, maybe that's a little bit. And I think also it's this culture of business, so very business-centric sort of culture. And again, it makes sense, the markets, you have less venture capital, you have less equity in the financial markets as well. And so, when you raise funding you need to have a strong business case. The business case is at the center of your habits. Whereas I think oftentimes in the U.S. you have, again, it's a little bit stereotypical, but it's a very tech or product-centric view of the world, or it can be a very tech or product-centric view of the world where it'll be like this product, this is the vision of the product, and sometimes even the business model will follow. And in France, I think the business model has to be front and center perhaps for you to be able to raise venture capital for you to be able to even exist. So, it means it attracts a lot of business minded entrepreneurs, much more so perhaps than tech-minded or product-minded entrepreneurs.
turns.zh: 或许是这样，或许只是一点点。我认为这也与商业文化有关，整体来说是一种非常以商业为中心的文化。再说，这也说得通——市场环境下，风险投资更少，金融市场的股权也更匮乏。因此，当你需要融资时，就必须拿出一个强有力的商业案例。商业案例是整个运营的核心。而在美国，人们往往有种刻板印象，认为那里更偏向于技术或产品导向的视角。产品是核心，商业模式有时甚至会随之而变。在法国，商业模式必须摆在首位，这样才能获得风险投资，才能让公司存续下去。因此，法国吸引了更多以商业为导向的创业者，或许比以技术或产品为导向的创业者还要多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. If someone wants to help their company in Europe and France operate more closely to the way companies in the U.S. operate, do you have any advice for them? I know you talk and work with a lot of companies in Europe, what do you help them change and see differently?
turns.zh: 我明白了。如果有人想让他们在欧洲和法国的公司更贴近美国公司的运营方式，你有什么建议吗？我知道你和很多欧洲公司合作过，你帮助他们做了哪些改变或获得了哪些不同的见解？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. I haven't fully cracked that, and think it's a really hard question. I'll give some sort of small pointers that have helped at least some of the companies that I've talked to. But the one is equity, I think there's a desire from a lot of the founders that I talk to, to give equity to employees, but because it's not in the culture yet I think employees also have an under-appreciation for equity. Like, "Well yeah, it's nice, but I don't know what's going to happen. I just work for the CEO anyways." There's less of this sense of, again, ownership that you can have in the U.S. (01:09:22): And so, I think leaning into that and investing in education around equity, the case is also in the U.S., I'm convinced 80% of people just don't fully understand their equity. But I think leaning into that, especially in Europe, to help people understand the value of their equity, help them by telling more about the story of the business, the trajectory of the business, why it matters for their future equity. I think anything along those lines I think can help cultivate this greater ownership mindset, I think for people. (01:09:58): And then yeah, I think another big piece again is, at least to me this is a big recipe to successful product teams, is to develop teams that revolve around this concept of ownership and accountability teams that are clearly owning a huge, or it doesn't have to be huge, like a slice of the business, not feature teams like shipping maybe guests, but teams that have clear accountability with consequences, but also clear ownership and leeway to do their best and to thrive.
turns.zh: 嗯，这是个很棒的问题。但我还没完全想明白，觉得这确实是个很难的问题。我能给出一些小建议，至少对一些我接触过的公司有帮助。比如股权问题，我发现很多创业者都想给员工股权，但由于这种文化尚未普及，员工对股权的价值认识不足。比如他们会想：“嗯，股权不错，但不知道未来会怎样，反正我还是为CEO工作。”在美国，人们能感受到更强的所有权意识。（01:09:22）所以，我认为要重视这一点，并加强股权教育。美国的情况也是如此，我相信80%的人根本不了解自己的股权。但我认为在欧洲尤其要重视这点，帮助人们理解股权的价值，讲清楚公司的业务规划、发展轨迹，以及股权对未来为何重要。只要能在这方面下功夫，就能培养出更强的所有权意识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Again, I usually don't spend time on this sort of thing, but I just think that what you're working on is extremely cool, and I think it's going to be really meaningful to a lot of people. And so, I just want to spend a few minutes giving you a chance to talk about what you're working on now. You started a company, is this your first company that you've started?
turns.zh: 再说，我通常不花时间谈这些，但我觉得你正在做的事情非常酷，对很多人都会有重大意义。所以，我想花几分钟时间，让你谈谈你现在在做什么。你创办了一家公司，这是你创办的第一家公司吗？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: It is, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，是第一家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It is first company.
turns.zh: 是第一家公司。

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: First real company. Doesn't accept projects, but first company.
turns.zh: 我的第一家真正的公司。虽然不接项目，但这毕竟是我的第一家公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's a LC, there's a C corp, or yeah, it's like filed. There's paperwork. Amazing. Talk about what you're building, how people know how to find it if it's right for them.
turns.zh: 是啊，有限责任公司（LLC），还有C类公司，或者说得更准确点，就是要去注册备案。得准备一堆文件材料。真是太棒了。能聊聊你正在打造的项目吗？要是它适合目标用户，他们该怎么才能找到它呢？

turns.speaker: Benjamin Lauzier
turns.en: Yeah, I have to say entrepreneurship has been a very humbling journey. I think the zero to one is way harder than anything us have done so far, and I feel like when you're used to building and scaling products within companies, you take for granted, at least I did, I take for granted that the problem space has already been validated. You have some brand equity, even if you launch a new vertical, there's an existing user base, there's a validation of the broader problem space. I think going to truly zero felt, at least to me, super overwhelming and lonely, but also super exciting with tons of condensed learnings. It's been a really interesting journey. So, what brought me there is my wife started to have some health issues about three years ago now, it's partially why we decided to move to France last year just for a couple of years. (01:11:47): And she's had this undiagnosed condition and chronic pain, and we saw just how much of a nightmare it was to manage her care and to navigate the healthcare system in the U.S. So, we'd wait three months for an appointment for a neurologist, then did see her for maybe eight minutes. Average appointment time in the U.S. is between 10 and 12 minutes. They'd dump a bunch of jargon, say like, "Hey, tests all look normal. Sorry, you should just go see this other specialist instead." Would wait another three months, see another specialist. And with a lot of anxiety, a lot of pain, as you can imagine, all those things, you have another eight minute slot with someone and you're like, "Oh, why didn't the neurologist do this test? I can help you, let's make some sense." And so, it ends up being incredibly isolating. The whole time we just felt completely alone. (01:12:32): It was just like us and Google, we felt we kept getting conflicting advice from doctors, and I was spending all my time researching specialists, what solutions to consider, spend all my nights reading through research papers to [inaudible 01:12:48], "Hey, what is the academic consensus on this particular treatment that the doctors don't seem to know about?" And throughout this whole process it felt like no one really had her back, no one within the medical system was fighting for her the way that your family doctor might have fought for you 20 years ago, knowing everything about you and being like, "Lenny, let's talk about this. I know your uncle had this," or there's this sort of a sense of advocacy that came from your family doctor that just doesn't exist today. It's not uncommon for doctors to have thousands of patients that they see just a few minutes each year. (01:13:19): And so digging into this, we just realized it's not an isolated case. You have nearly half of Americans have at least one chronic condition, or have to deal with some sort of complex health issue largely on their own. You see a lot of those large online communities revolving around chronic conditions or chronic pain, and trying to make sense of it and advocate for themselves. And I think I want to be clear, in my mind the problem is obviously not about the practitioners, it's systemic. It's just growing financial pressure from private equity firms, it's just countless other factors. But you see the physicians being overwhelmed, overworked, burning out, and you see that pressure just only increasing, I think. So, I basically spent the next six months just talking to hundreds of patients, and doctors, and experts, and what we built is basically a platform to help people fight for their health. (01:14:12): And so, we want to close the gap between patients and the healthcare system. There's this critical layer of the system that's missing, I think, people are navigating life-threatening or debilitating conditions largely with Google, and at some point you just get tired of fighting for yourself. So, we connect people with complex conditions, typically with their own health advocate. So, it's essentially like their own health assistant. They're available 24/7 to help you navigate your care. So, we find appointments for you, we help you prepare your appointment, we make sense of a diagnosis, of test results. We spend hours researching solutions and potential treatments, and just more generally we do everything we can to help you just better advocate for themselves basically. And now we launched in the U.S. a early version of this few weeks ago, and the engagement has been really, really, really mind-blowing so far. And we're helping cancer patients, people with a lot of those niche chronic conditions, and literally harassing the doctor's office like, "Hey, we still haven't received that referral." (01:15:15): All the things that you just get tired of doing when you're dealing with so many appointments, and when you're having to manage a condition like this. And our mental model is what would we do if this user was our partner or our parent? You'd likely spend all night combing through research. You'd call all the providers in the state to be like, "Hey, who has an appointment?" Because there's no PT available for the next two months. We'll find you a PT available sooner. So, we're building the engine to do that at scale essentially, and make people feel like they're not alone and that someone is fighting for them.
turns.zh:
是啊，我不得不说创业之路实在令人谦卑。我觉得从零到一的挑战远比我们迄今为止所做过的任何事情都要难得多。当你习惯了在公司内开发和扩展产品时，会理所当然地认为问题空间已经得到了验证。即便你开拓新业务领域，也能依托现有品牌资产，利用已有的用户基础，借助更广泛的问题验证。但真正从零开始创业，至少对我而言，感觉无比压抑和孤立无援，同时又充满了浓缩的学习机会。这是一段非常有趣的旅程。

推动我踏上这条路的契机，是三年前我的妻子开始出现健康问题。正是这个原因，我们去年决定搬到法国，暂住几年。（01:11:47）她患有未确诊的疾病和慢性疼痛，我们亲身经历了在美国管理她的医疗护理和医疗系统是多么的痛苦。例如，预约神经科医生要等三个月，实际诊疗时间只有八分钟。而美国的平均诊疗时间是10到12分钟。医生们只会抛出一堆专业术语，比如“检查结果正常，对不起，你应该去看别的专家”。然后再等三个月，换个专家看病。在焦虑和疼痛中煎熬时，你只能再花八分钟跟医生沟通，心想：“为什么神经科医生不做这个检查？我可以帮忙分析啊！”整个过程令人感到无比孤立。我们始终觉得自己被遗弃了。（01:12:32）这就像我们面对谷歌时，医生给出的建议相互矛盾。我整天都在研究专家，寻找可行的解决方案，晚上通宵阅读研究论文，问：“针对医生们不知道的特定治疗方案，学术界的共识是什么？” 整个过程中，似乎没人真正为她出头——医疗系统里没有人像20年前家庭医生那样了解你的全部情况，说：“伦尼，我们来聊聊这个。我知道你叔叔也遇到过类似情况。”如今这种为患者代言的医患关系早已不复存在。医生每年要面对数千名患者，每次诊疗仅几分钟，这很常见。（01:13:19）深入调查后我们发现，这并非个例。近半数美国人至少患有一种慢性病，或不得不独自应对复杂的健康问题。网上有很多围绕慢性病或慢性疼痛的社区，大家试图理解病情并为自己争取权益。我想明确一点，问题显然不在于医生个人，根源在于系统性问题。比如私募股权公司日益增长的财务压力，还有其他诸多因素。但你能看到医生们被压得喘不过气、过度劳累、身心俱疲，而这种压力似乎还在不断加剧。因此，接下来六个月我与数百名患者、医生和专家交流，最终搭建了一个帮助人们为健康抗争的平台。（01:14:12）我们希望缩小患者与医疗系统之间的鸿沟。
医疗保健系统。我认为，这个系统中存在一个至关重要的缺失环节——人们大多是通过谷歌来应对危及生命或使人衰弱的健康问题，而当你为自己的健康持续抗争到疲惫不堪时，总会有个临界点。所以，我们为患有复杂疾病的患者牵线搭桥，通常会为他们配备专属的健康顾问。这实质上就是他们的私人健康助手——这些顾问全天候为患者提供护理指导。我们帮患者预约就诊、准备就诊资料、解读诊断报告和检查结果。我们会花数小时研究治疗方案，总之竭尽全力帮助患者更好地为自己争取权益。几周前，我们在美国推出了这款服务的初版版本，目前用户反响热烈，令人惊喜。我们正在帮助癌症患者、患有各种罕见慢性病的人群，甚至会主动催促医生办公室：“嘿，我们还没收到转诊通知呢！” （01:15:15）这些都是患者在频繁预约、应对复杂病情时容易感到疲惫的琐事。而我们的思维模式是——如果这位用户是我们的伴侣或父母，我们会怎么做？很可能整夜查阅资料，挨个联系全州的医疗机构，询问：“嘿，谁能给我预约个治疗师？” 因为下个月的理疗名额都满了。我们要搭建一个大规模的支持体系，让人们感受到自己并不孤单，总有人在为他们而努力。

(01:17:55): So, if you feel this way, this is a good book to make you feel a little bit better by yourself and your imposter syndrome. At least it did for me.
